scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Rake-and-scrape developed in The Bahamas as an Afro-Bahamian tradition rooted in the 19th century.
Early documentation places the genre's scraped rhythms in Nassau as far back as 1864, when Frank Wilson remarked on the grating sounds of the rasp and saw.
Subsequent historical records from the late 19th century describe ensembles featuring hollow logs, drums, fifes, banjos, triangles, and accordions across Nassau, Long Cay, and other settlements.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Rake-and-scrape serves as a foundational expression of Bahamian cultural identity, standing alongside Junkanoo as the nation's traditional sound.

Historically performed at post-wedding feasts and community celebrations, it reflects the resourcefulness of Afro-Bahamian communities who repurposed functional everyday tools into rich cultural expression.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The musical dynamics of rake-and-scrape rely on a signature ensemble trio: the hand saw scraped with a metal rod, the goat- or sheep-skin Goombay drum, and the accordion or concertina.
Historical variants incorporated secondary and alternative instruments, such as the banjo, fife, guitar, tambourine, triangle, washbasin tub, and harmonica.
Listen for the hand saw, Goombay drum, accordion, concertina.

Rake-and-scrape music is characterized by the distinct, rasping metallic scraping of a hand saw combined with the resonant strike of a goat-skin Goombay drum. Melodic leads are provided by an accordion or concertina, supported by background rhythmic strumming from acoustic guitars or banjos.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Prominent figures and contemporary artists associated with rake-and-scrape music include Kirkland KB Bodie, Geno D, Ancient Man, Ronnie Butler, Stevie S, Clay "Qpid" Adderley, Sharmond Smith, and Phil Stubbs.

Historical field recordings captured early formal saw playing by ensembles such as the Fresh Creek Dance Band of Andros in 1959, while broadcaster Charles Carter documented Cat Island practitioners in 1969.
Regional variations developed across the Bahamian archipelago.

The lineage of rake-and-scrape traces back to 19th-century Goombay traditions in The Bahamas, merging African percussive scraping and drumming concepts with European melody instruments like the concertina and fife.
